title: Google replaces search button with 3 Gemini shortcuts in global homepage redesign
summary: Google replaces its search button with three Gemini shortcuts in global homepage redesign
detailed: Google is globally redesigning its desktop homepage, replacing the traditional 'Google Search' button with three Gemini-powered shortcuts: Nano Banana, file uploads, and 'Brainstorm'.
A new Gemini sidebar has been introduced to give users direct access to recent AI conversations, tasks, and chat history.
Conventional web search functionality and the 'I'm Feeling Lucky' button remain fully intact alongside the updated interface.
This matters as it shifts AI capabilities from hidden attachment menus to the primary gateway of Google's search ecosystem.
sentences: Google is redesigning its iconic desktop homepage, replacing the traditional ‘Google Search’ button with three dedicated entry points to its Gemini-powered features, as the company expands the visibility of its artificial intelligence offerings across its core search platform.
The changes, which are being rolled out globally, introduce shortcuts for image generation through Nano Banana, file uploads and a ‘Brainstorm’ feature powered by Gemini.
The redesigned homepage also includes a sidebar that allows users to access their recent AI Mode conversations and start new chats.
The move marks a change in how Google is positioning its homepage, bringing AI-led tasks closer to the starting point of users' online activity.

While the traditional search functionality remains intact, the removal of the dedicated search button signals a shift in the prominence given to AI-powered experiences within Google's primary consumer interface.
Robby Stein, Vice President of Product for Google Search, announced the redesign on X.
The changes bring features that were previously accessible through the attachment menu beside the search bar directly onto the homepage.

Three Gemini entry points replace the traditional search button
The three new shortcuts are designed around distinct AI-powered tasks.
Nano Banana allows users to generate images, while the file upload option enables them to submit documents for Gemini to process.
The third option, ‘Brainstorm’, provides an entry point for users looking to explore ideas and work through open-ended queries using Gemini.
Previously, these capabilities were housed within the attachment menu, accessible through the '+' icon beside the search bar.
Their placement on the homepage makes them more immediately visible to desktop users without requiring them to navigate through additional menus.
The redesign also retains Google's ‘I'm Feeling Lucky’ button, even as the conventional ‘Google Search’ button is phased out.
Alongside the new shortcuts, Google has introduced a Gemini sidebar that provides access to recent AI conversations, tasks and a new chat option.
This gives users a direct route back to their previous interactions instead of requiring them to initiate a fresh session each time they visit the homepage.

The addition of conversation history also extends Gemini's presence beyond individual search interactions, placing ongoing AI-assisted activities within the same interface that users traditionally associate with web discovery.

Traditional search remains, but homepage priorities are changing
Despite the visual overhaul, Google's conventional search functionality is not being discontinued.
Users can continue entering queries into the search bar and pressing Enter or Return to access regular search results.
AI Mode is accessed separately through its designated interface, rather than automatically replacing conventional results for every query.
The distinction is significant as the redesign changes the prominence of Google's AI tools without fundamentally altering the existing search mechanism.
The development also follows Google's earlier experiments with introducing AI Mode more prominently across its search experience.

The company has progressively integrated AI-powered capabilities into Search, including features that allow users to move beyond conventional keyword-based queries and engage with more conversational forms of information discovery.
Google's homepage has historically served as the primary gateway to its search ecosystem.
Bringing image generation, document analysis and brainstorming capabilities directly to this interface expands its role beyond directing users to external webpages.
For the digital advertising and publishing ecosystem, the development comes amid Google's broader integration of AI into search and information discovery.
However, the homepage redesign, by itself, does not establish any change to the advertising model, search ranking systems or the visibility of publisher links.

The immediate change is therefore one of interface and accessibility: Gemini's capabilities are receiving more prominent placement, while the familiar search experience continues to operate alongside them.
